diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
I'm making one small change, a 32-word unrolled block ahead of the 16-word one. It is untested and the expected gain is small.

The cost is the number of SSA instructions executed. The current code already needs about 4 per word: an `IndexAddr`, a load, a call to `bits.OnesCount64`, and an add. The gap between the reference cost (7570) and this program (4343) suggests `OnesCount64` is cheap in giri, probably counted as a single call. I considered a hand-written SWAR popcount that would sum partial counts across words before the final reduction. If `OnesCount64` is cheap, that would cost about 10 instructions per word and lose, so I am not using it.

What remains is the per-iteration overhead of the `len(xs) >= 16` check and the `xs = xs[16:]` reslice. A 32-word block pays that overhead half as often on long inputs. The existing 16-word loop becomes an `if`, so it handles the remainder. Correctness is unchanged, because every block still covers exactly the words it consumes.
